newsitem.title: USA: Alhambra, Calif., files $50 mln claim over traffic.
newsitem.headline: Alhambra, Calif., files $50 mln claim over traffic.

text.p: Alhambra, Calif., filed a $50 million claim against federal transportation officials over their alleged failure to proceed with a major freeway construction project, city officials said on Wednesday.

City officials said the claim alleged that transportation officials discriminated against the city's minority residents by failing to permit the completion of a 6.2-mile gap in Interstate 710, the Long Beach Freeway.
The city said the gap has put 100,000 vehicles daily on Alhambra streets, creating 4.8 tons of carbon monoxide each day. The city said its ethnic minorities are hardest hit.
The claim names as defendants U.S. Secretary of Transportation Federico Pena and Director of the Federal Highway Administration Rodney Slater, the city said.

The California Highway Commission adopted the freeway route for Interstate 710 in 1964. The freeway was completed except for the 6.2-mile gap, which was blocked through legal maneuvers by the city of South Pasadena.

In 1973, the state agreed not to proceed with the final segment until an environmental impact statement was completed and approved by the U.S. Department of Transportation. The environmental impact statement was completed in 1992 and released for public comment, and now awaits signatures by Secretary Pena and Director Slater on a record of decision.

"Their failure to do so in a timely manner is the basis for this claim," Alhambra said in a statement. The city said it filed a suit in U.S. District Court, asking the court to order Pena and Slater to sign the record of decision.

In a separate action, the city filed suit in U.S. District Court challenging the federal approval of funding and construction of southern California's Alameda Corridor, a massive project that would consolidate about 90 miles of existing rail into a single, 20-mile high capacity line.
The city alleged in the Alameda Corridor suit that federal and state transportation officials failed to fully consider the potential impacts of the massive project on Alhambra.
